_doc: The on-site tour of Prairie Avenue (T-3674): a walk on today's street, holding a phone or tablet in Window mode, through seven stops of the 1700 to 1900 blocks to the Glessner House. renderers/web/js/onsite.js runs it; tools/check_onsite_tour.mjs holds it. Each stop's lat/lon is where the visitor stands TODAY: the middle of the walk band in front of its 1904 parcel's street front (data/street_grid/1904.json, from the 1911 Sanborn sheets), carried to today's ground through the 1904 registration (renderers/web/js/today-register.js) and turned to WGS84 by today-geo.js. The check re-derives every position from its parcel and holds the last against the City's own landmark lot for 1800 S. Prairie. Every factual line of a stop's text is one of the existing records it names under `evidence` (a jaunt's evidence row or a 1904 household), and its `sources` are theirs; `citations` copies each source's citation verbatim from data/sources/. The route, its order and its stands are modern interpretation (L-onsite-prairie-1904); no visit in 1904 is asserted.
title: Prairie Avenue on foot
premise: Seven stops on today's Prairie Avenue, 18th Street to the 1900 block and back, ending at the Glessner House. Stand where each stop says and look through the screen at the street as it stood in 1904.

stops.title: The Pullman house

stand.walk: the east walk, north of 18th Street

stops.text: George M. Pullman's mansion, built 1870 to 1876, with a theatre of about 200 seats, a pipe organ and a bowling alley, the district marker says. Pullman died in 1897; the 1904 Blue Book lists his widow here. He had complained of the house across the corner: 'I do not know what I have ever done to have that thing staring me in the face every time I go out of my door'. Razed 1922.

stops.title: The Kimball house
stops.text: W. W. Kimball's house, built 1890 to Solon S. Beman's design 'in the French Chateauesque style' for the piano and organ maker, the district marker says. Kimball started in Chicago in 1857, 'beginning with only four pianos'. The 1904 Blue Book lists the Kimballs here; he 'died at his home in Chicago on December 16, 1904'.

stops.title: The Coleman house
stops.text: Joseph G. Coleman's house, built 1886 by Cobb & Frost, 'well known for their designs in the Romanesque style, executed here in rough-faced brown sandstone' (the district marker). A plate of 1888 shows its deep round arch on clustered columns over a broad stair, and a corbelled oriel over the arch.

stops.title: Marshall Field's house

stand.walk: the east walk, a block south

stops.text: Built in 1876 and called 'the first in Chicago to be completely wired for electricity'; its plans came from the office of Richard Morris Hunt. The 1904 Blue Book lists Marshall Field here, 'the wealthiest and most powerful businessman in Chicago'. Razed 1955.

stops.title: The Elbridge Keith house

stand.walk: the west walk, across the avenue

stops.text: Built 1870 to John W. Roberts's design. The district marker calls it 'the last surviving example of the popular Second Empire style, which dominated the street by the 1880s'. The 1904 Blue Book lists the Elbridge G. Keiths here; the 1900 census calls him a bank president.

stops.title: The Keith house
stops.text: The Inland Architect announced it in September 1886: 'For O. R. Keith, three story dwelling, 38 by 80 feet, 1808 Prairie avenue, granite front; cost $40,000.' The 1904 Blue Book lists Mr. and Mrs. Stanley Field here. When it was pulled down in 1968, its north wall was kept to preserve the Glessner House's private courtyard.

stops.title: The Glessner House

stand.walk: the west walk, at the corner of 18th Street

stops.text: Henry Hobson Richardson's last work, its street walls faced in granite. He held that the windows of a city house were 'not to look out of'; a 1958 plaque praised the plan 'which opens the family rooms to the quiet serenity of an inner yard'. John J. Glessner, of the farm-machinery firm Warder, Bushnell & Glessner, and his wife Frances first slept here on 1 December 1887, and live here in 1904.
